segments: "Once you are comfortable with these tools, you will be able to ‘rewrite the past’ and ‘select precisely which changes to keep.’"
1. Rebasing: git rebase
At its core, rebase means changing the base of a branch.
Comparing the philosophies: Merge vs. Rebase
Explanation:
Merge: Preserves the ancestry of the branches and produces a new merge point, M1. The history reflects what actually happened, but with many branches, the graph can become a tangled web.

Rebase: Takes the feature branch's commit D and “reapplies” it using the latest commit on master, C, as its new base. The resulting D' replays the same patch, though conflict resolution and the new base may change the final contents; its hash also changes because its parent pointer has changed. The history becomes a straight line.
Scenario: keeping a feature branch up to date
You are working on the feature branch, while master has moved ahead.
The Merge approach: Preserves the divergence between branches and may create a merge commit.

The Rebase approach:
git switch feature/example
git rebase master
The golden rule: do not rebase public branches!
The technical reason: hash fission
Changing the parent: When you rebase, you create new commits with different parent relationships. The original commit objects are not modified in place.
The chain reaction: A hash is generated from the contents, including the parent hash. When the parent hash changes, the commit's hash changes completely as well, becoming D'.
Breaking history: If you push D' to a shared remote branch, other collaborators still have the old D history locally, and you need to coordinate a common base.

The resulting mess: When a colleague runs git pull, Git sees D locally and D' remotely. Because their hashes differ, Git treats them as two distinct histories. If your colleague tries to merge them, this can produce many duplicate commits and messy conflicts.
In short: rebase only branches that are “your own.” On shared branches, stick to Merge.
2. Cherry-picking: git cherry-pick
Scenario: You have written 10 commits on the dev branch, but an urgent release needs just one specific feature, such as Commit X, on master.
Git normally applies the changes introduced by that commit to the current branch and creates a new commit; conflicts are possible. To cherry-pick a merge commit, specify the mainline parent with -m.
3. Interactive rebasing: git rebase -i
This is “surgery” for rewriting history. It lets you combine, rename, or even remove past commits.
Common commands in the editor:
pick: Keep the commit.
reword: Keep the commit, but change its commit message.
edit: Stop to let you modify the code.
squash: Combine commits. Fold this commit into the previous one, often to clean up a messy series of WIP commits.
drop: Skip the commit in the new history. Whether the old object remains available depends on references, reflogs, and GC.
4. Reference logs: git reflog (the ultimate rescue tool)
Scenario: You accidentally ran git reset --hard or lost code during a rebase.

The local reflog records reference updates, and the HEAD reflog can also record checkouts. Entries expire and are not automatically transferred to a remote by normal fetch/push operations. It cannot guarantee recovery of uncommitted content.
5. Finding bugs: git bisect (binary search)
Scenario: Your project suddenly has an error, and you do not know which day or commit introduced it.
Interrupting operations and verifying the result

If a rebase or cherry-pick encounters conflicts, check status, edit and stage the conflicted files, then use git rebase --continue or git cherry-pick --continue, respectively. To abandon the operation, use its corresponding --abort option. rebase -i HEAD~3 requires that ancestor to exist; use --root for a range including the initial commit.

bisect requires a reproducible good/bad test. Use git bisect skip for commits that cannot be tested in your environment; skipping multiple commits may leave more than one possible culprit. When finished, run git bisect reset to return to your position before the search.
